summary: Victor S. Limlingan argues that the Philippines should create a Philippine Education Development Fund (PhilEd), modeled on PhilHealth, by folding in the existing FAPE/PEAC structure and funds and the DepEd's private-education subsidy programs. PhilEd would fund Filipinos' three education dreams: vouchers, insurance of pre-need educational plans, and lifelong learning organizations. He also proposes funding sources like extractive industry taxes and documentary stamp collections, and urges Congress to pass a Universal Education Financing Law.
one_line: Victor Limlingan proposes creating PhilEd, a PhilHealth-like education fund built from FAPE/PEAC, to fund vouchers, insure educational plans and create lifelong learning organizations.
key_facts: A paper at the 5th Paderanga-Varela Memorial Lecture, "Alternate Service Delivery Systems: Health and Education," concluded that the DoH's service delivery system is far superior to DepEd's.
The DoH devolved its hospitals to local government units and spun off health financing into PhilHealth, while DepEd has done neither.
PhilEd would take over the School Vouchers Program from DepEd and insure pre-need educational plans like PDIC insures bank deposits, funded by premiums from plan companies.
PhilEd would partner with international development agencies and the private sector to create Lifelong Learning Organizations (LLOs), acting as the "bastonero" or project manager.

FAPE was part of the Special Fund for Education set aside by the American government in 1963 from War Damage Act of 1962 surplus funds, organized under Executive Order 156 issued by President Ferdinand Marcos on Nov. 5, 1968.
FAPE's seed money was $6,154,000 or P215 million at the 1968 exchange rate, and it had barely grown to P277 million in 55 years.
PEAC was spun off from FAPE and co-implements DepEd programs including ESC, TSS, SHS Voucher Program, INSET and Bayanihan for Basic Education.
Folding FAPE/PEAC into PhilEd would transfer FAPE's P277 million and PEAC's assets and liabilities of P567 million, both as of May 31, 2022.
PEAC-managed DepEd programs to move to PhilEd: ESC P9.3 billion, SHS Voucher Program P20.3 billion, and Teachers' Salaries Subsidy P793 million, all for School Year 2021-2022.

The current FAPE Board of Trustees, chaired by the Secretary of Education with the NEDA Director-General and presidents of ACSCU, CEAP and PACU, would become PhilEd's board, with PEAC's management team incoming.
PhilHealth received P74 billion in sin taxes in Fiscal Year 2022, and P188 billion in 2022 from 50% of PAGCOR's government share and 40% of PCSO's Charity Fund under the Universal Health Care Law.
Limlingan suggests PhilEd get a share of extractive industry taxes, a percentage of documentary stamp collections, and access to local Special Education Funds.
PhilHealth was created by Republic Act 7875, the National Health Insurance Act of 1995; the author hopes Congress will file a Universal Education Financing Law to create PhilEd.
